tabs.title: Observing Asteroids
tabs.description: Explain how scientists learn about uncertain paths.

tabs.title: Lessons from Events
tabs.description: Evaluate real examples and their limits.

tabs.title: Evidence and Preparation
tabs.description: Apply the article's argument to new claims.

questions.q: Why are ancient asteroids useful objects for scientific study?
choices: They contain the first photographs of Earth.
They prove that all planets are the same age.
They show exactly when the Sun will disappear.
They preserve clues to the solar system's distant past.
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph says asteroids are leftovers from the early solar system.

questions.q: What is the risk of predicting an asteroid's route from only one photograph?
choices: The photograph will always show the wrong asteroid.
There is too little information to know its path confidently.
Computers cannot calculate orbits from images.
An asteroid never follows the same orbit twice.
questions.explanation: The text explains why several observations are required before confident predictions.

questions.q: Why might astronomers change an earlier prediction?
choices: The object's scientific name is changed.
The rock has stopped following the Sun.
New measurements improve the estimated orbit.
A different news site has reported it.
questions.explanation: Additional observations can alter estimates, particularly soon after discovery.

questions.q: Why was the DART mission a useful test rather than an emergency rescue?
choices: Its target posed no actual impact threat to Earth.
It was carried out without scientific observations.
The spacecraft never reached the target.
The experiment tried to destroy the asteroid belt.
questions.explanation: Paragraph three explicitly says the mission was a controlled test with a safe target.

questions.q: What made the Chelyabinsk explosion dangerous even without a large crater?
choices: The asteroid landed in the city centre.
It destroyed a large part of the Moon.
Its light made people unable to breathe.
The shock wave broke windows and injured people.
questions.explanation: The blast's shock wave caused injury, mostly through flying glass.

questions.q: Why was this particular space rock hard to spot before it arrived?
choices: It never moved through the atmosphere.
It came from the Sun's direction.
It was hidden beneath the ground.
It flew only at night.
questions.explanation: Bright sunlight hid the incoming small object from telescopes.

questions.q: A headline says, 'An asteroid will pass near Earth tomorrow!' What would the writer advise?
choices: Check what 'near' means before becoming afraid.
Assume a collision is already certain.
Ignore all information from astronomers.
Conclude that space surveys are useless.
questions.explanation: The closing paragraph calls for clear explanations that avoid unnecessary fear.

questions.q: What is the advantage of finding a dangerous object early?
choices: The object will automatically move away.
The risk can no longer be measured.
Scientists may have more time to choose a response.
It makes the asteroid easier to see without equipment.
questions.explanation: The text identifies early warning as valuable alongside possible spacecraft solutions.

questions.q: Which conclusion about DART would go beyond the evidence described?
choices: A collision can change an orbit in some circumstances.
It has already proved Earth can be protected from any asteroid.
Scientists can conduct a controlled planetary-defence experiment.
The smaller body completed its orbit more quickly afterwards.
questions.explanation: The text says only a small change was demonstrated in a specific safe experiment.

questions.q: Why does the writer favour international cooperation?
choices: Different countries need their own separate asteroid belts.
Only one country can observe each object.
It makes space rocks stop following the Sun.
Shared measurements and warnings make preparation more effective.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph links international cooperation and accurate information with better decisions.
